stories.headline: Week 4 winners and losers: CeeDee Lamb, Kyren Williams dominate; Jaxon Smith-Njigba struggles
stories.summary: CeeDee Lamb and Kyren Williams came up big in Week 4, while Jaxon Smith-Njigba and D'Andre Swift had a disappointing day.
stories.byline: Matt Bowen and Tristan H. Cockcroft
stories.body:
Week 4 of the 2026 fantasy football season featured massive games by CeeDee Lamb, Kyren Williams and Javonte Williams. On the flip side, Jaxon Smith-Njigba, D'Andre Swift and Trevor Lawrence had disappointing outings.

Who were the big winners and losers around the league during the fourth week of the fantasy football season?

Matt Bowen and Tristan H. Cockcroft offer their analysis.

Jump to a topic:

Ranking winners | Ranking losers

Biggest injuries and what's next

Ranking fantasy winners of Week 4
1. CeeDee Lamb, WR, Dallas Cowboys
What a day by the star wide receiver and -- in fact -- a career-best performance in terms of targets (21), catches (17) and fantasy points (41.3). The Texans' defense, which relies on zone coverage more than any team in the league, had no answers for Lamb's elite ability as he managed 14 catches for 161 yards in zone coverage and had the game-winning, 14-yard touchdown with 43 seconds remaining. He should continue to serve as a locked-in fantasy WR1 against the Buccaneers next week. -- Cockcroft

2. Kyren Williams, RB, Los Angeles Rams
Williams scored a season-high 36.7 points in Sunday's win over the Rams, rushing for 80 yards and two scores on 16 carries, plus he had 10 receptions for 67 yards. Sure, game flow contributed to Williams' usage as a receiver, but he has scored at least 21 points in two straight games. With a positive matchup versus the Bills up next, Williams should be played as an RB1. -- Bowen

3. Javonte Williams, RB, Dallas Cowboys
Williams dropped a season-high 31.3 points on the Texans' defense in Week 4, rushing for three touchdowns (on goal-to-goal carries), while producing 83 total yards on 24 touches. Williams has at least 18 points, and a rushing score, in three of four games this season. With his steady low red zone usage (11 goal-to-go carries on the season) in a high-scoring Dallas offense, Williams fit as a lower-tier RB1 for the Week 5 game versus Tampa Bay. -- Bowen

4. Kenneth Walker III, RB, Kansas City Chiefs
Walker continues to post elite RB1 numbers in Andy Reid's offense. Walker scored 30.9 points in Sunday's win over the Chiefs, rushing for 177 yards and two touchdowns on 22 carries, while adding one reception for two yards. Walker is now scoring 27.5 PPG, and he has at least one touchdown in every game played. Walker should be viewed as a top-3 running back when the Chiefs return from the bye in Week 6 versus the Chargers. -- Bowen

5. Nico Collins, WR, Houston Texans
Collins, who missed the past two games because of a hamstring injury, scored a season-high 30.8 points in the loss to Dallas, catching seven of a team-high eight targets for 110 yards and two touchdowns. The difference-maker for the Texans' pass game, Collins caught both of his touchdowns on end zone throws from quarterback C.J. Stroud. Collins is a WR1 for the Week 5 matchup at Tennessee. -- Bowen

6. Zay Flowers, WR, Baltimore Ravens
Flowers scored a season-high 25.8 points in the Week 4 win over the Titans, catching eight of 10 targets for 118 yards and a score. However, where do we see Flowers in the Week 5 matchup versus the Falcons if Lamar Jackson (ankle) can't play? If Tyler Huntley starts, look for more play-action throws, which will create schemed targets for Flowers. He'll stay in the WR2 range. -- Bowen

7. Kyle Monangai, RB, Chicago Bears
The Bears' rushing standout of Week 4, Monangai handled seven goal-to-go carries and converted two for touchdowns, and effectively took over the backfield during the second half on his way to a career-best 28.0 fantasy point total. Whether D'Andre Swift's goal-line struggles or third-quarter fumble influenced the shift (more on that below) or whether the thumb injury Monangai apparently suffered during the game will be a lingering issue, will have plenty to say on how touches are doled out by coach Ben Johnson. Assuming full health for both players for Week 5, Swift and Monangai both warrant RB2/flex consideration against a Packers defense that has been getting clobbered by running backs thus far (29.0 FPPG). -- Cockcroft

8. Malik Nabers, WR, New York Giants
There's the fantasy WR1-caliber performance we've all been hoping for from Nabers, a performance that seemed more of a distant hope after Jameis Winston took over at quarterback for the injured Jaxson Dart. Nabers had a 24% target share and 23.2 fantasy points here, which come at a good time, considering he has another favorable, high-end WR2-caliber matchup in Week 5 against the Commanders. -- Cockcroft

9. Drake Maye, QB, and Romeo Doubs, WR, New England Patriots
The duo showed good chemistry for the first time this year, as Maye scored 26.16 fantasy points and Doubs scored 23.8, which for each was more than he totaled from Weeks 1-3 combined (Maye 21.60, Doubs 20.5). Though Maye threw another interception -- he is one (7) away from his 2025 total (8) -- he was much improved on deeper throws, going 10-for-17 for 174 yards and two touchdowns when throwing at least 10 yards downfield, per Next Gen Stats. It's a good sign for both, considering they'll face the Raiders and Jets -- two teams that have overperformed against wide receivers thus far -- in Weeks 5 and 6. Maye is a borderline standard-league starter, and Doubs is a WR3/flex for those games. -- Cockcroft

10. Tee Higgins, WR, Cincinnati Bengals
Thrust into the spotlight after Ja'Marr Chase's (concussion) early exit, Higgins dominated targets with 16 of the team's 53 and finished with 26.7 fantasy points. Higgins would elevate to Joe Burrow's No. 1 receiving target against the Dolphins next week should Chase either not clear the league protocol or be held out to give rest through the team's Week 6 bye. -- Cockcroft

11. Emanuel Wilson, RB, Seattle Seahawks
With Jadarian Price (chest) on injured reserve, Wilson capitalized by playing 59% of the offensive snaps, handling 21-of-33 rushing attempts and totaling 27.0 fantasy points. That Wilson had three catches for 33 yards and a score while running only one fewer route (8) than did George Holani (9) also speaks well for his newfound status as the team's No. 1 back. He's unlikely to be a league-winner, especially not with tricky matchups ahead (SF, @DEN, KC), but the usage signals fantasy RB2/flex utility. -- Cockcroft

12. T.J. Hockenson, TE, Minnesota Vikings
Hockenson scored a season-high 24.9 points in Sunday's win over the Dolphins, catching all 13 of his targets for 119 yards. If Justin Jefferson (ankle) is still down next week, Hockenson should be started in a prime matchup versus a Saints' defense that has struggled against opposing tight ends. -- Bowen

13. Quinshon Judkins, RB, Cleveland Browns
In the Thursday night game, Judkins had a season-high 21.6 points in the win over the Steelers. Judkins had 17 carries, rushing for 53 yards and a score. Plus, he posted a season-best six receptions for 43 yards. With the downhill run game volume in the Browns' system and a boost in receiving usage, Judkins can be played as a solid RB2 in a positive Week 5 matchup versus the Jets' defense. -- Bowen

Ranking fantasy losers of Week 4
1. D'Andre Swift, RB, Chicago Bears
He failed to convert on three goal-to-go carries early in Week 4, then fumbled early in the third quarter and didn't play again. Swift finished with 7.4 fantasy points, meaning he has scored fewer points in his past three games (31.1) than he did in Week 1 (32.4). Backfield partner Kyle Monangai suffered an apparent thumb injury in what was a breakout game, however, so we'll see whether Swift is needed to handle the lion's share of the rushing work in a favorable Week 5 matchup against the Packers. -- Cockcroft

2. Jaxon Smith-Njigba, WR, Seattle Seahawks
Perhaps we're spoiled when a wide receiver can score 12.6 fantasy points for us and still be termed a disappointment, but here we are. Smith-Njigba saw only six targets, but the Seahawks also didn't need to lean heavily upon him with a big lead for most of the day -- Sam Darnold attempted only 22 passes total. Even with the so-so score, Smith-Njigba has 116.66 fantasy points through four games, a total exceeded by only 15 other players (at any position) this century and 19 since the merger. He's off to one heck of a start and will be a critical part of the game plan against the 49ers next week. -- Cockcroft

3. Travis Kelce, TE, Kansas City Chiefs
His modest usage finally came back to haunt him, as after he turned five or fewer targets into at least 10 fantasy points in two of his first three games (with the other an 11-target, 25.1 point Week 2), Kelce saw only four passes and scored 3.5 points on Sunday. At this stage of his career, he's more apt to be a hit-or-miss type than the top-shelf option he was during his prime. Kelce and the Chiefs have their bye in Week 5. -- Cockcroft

4. Trevor Lawrence, QB, Jacksonville Jaguars
Lawrence (13.08 points) was efficient throwing the ball in the Week 4 win over the Bengals (18 of 23, 227 yards), but he finished with only one touchdown pass, and he didn't record a rushing yard on three carries. The rushing totals have been down for Lawrence this season (8.5 yards per game), which is a concern after he averaged 21.1 yards per game in 2025. Lawrence and the Jags get the Eagles' defense in Week 5. ---Bowen

5. Parker Washington, WR, Jacksonville Jaguars
He was the 15th most-started wide receiver in ESPN leagues (76.7%), but Washington was held to a perplexing three targets and 2.0 points by the Bengals. Credit the Bengals' secondary, which is better than you think thanks to the play of CBs DJ Turner II and Dax Hill. Washington should rebound with WR2/3 fantasy numbers against the Eagles in Week 5, though the Dolphins' wideouts should be avoided, considering WR1s have averaged only 8.0 fantasy points against the Bengals thus far. -- Cockcroft

6. Dalton Kincaid, TE, Buffalo Bills
Kincaid was a nonfactor in the loss to the Patriots. Kincaid had two targets, catching one for 7 yards (1.7 points), and he has caught just three of five for 45 yards in his past two games. Big drop-off here for Kincaid, who scored 20.3 PPG in his first two games of the season. Kincaid is still seeing usage in the route tree (18.5 routes run over the past two games), so he'll look to get back on track in Week 5 versus the Rams. ---Bowen

7. Trey McBride, TE, Arizona Cardinals
McBride had heavy usage (12 targets) in Sunday's game, and he caught seven passes. However, McBride totaled only 31 yards receiving (10.1 points). I'm not concerned about McBride though, as he has had double-digit targets in all four games this season. And the Lions' defense is up next in Week 5. -- Bowen

8. Jeremiyah Love, RB, Arizona Cardinals
Love scored 6.5 points in the Week 4 loss to the Giants, rushing for 63 yards on 14 carries, while catching one pass for minus-8 yards. And Tyler Allgeier got some more work, too (49 total yards, 10 touches, one touchdown). It was a rough day for the rookie, a week after posting a season-high 21.9 points on the 49ers' defense. Love will look to rebound in a positive matchup next week versus the Lions. -- Bowen

9. Garrett Wilson, WR, New York Jets
A top-25 started player overall in ESPN leagues (92.9%), Wilson was practically invisible against the Bears, running 18 routes but finishing with only four targets and 5.7 fantasy points. The Jets' paltry 17:15 time of possession -- that's the least by any team in 2026 -- had a lot to do with it, but the team also entered the week with two of the three largest numbers in the category this season, and the Jets get the Browns in Week 5. A WR1-caliber rebound should be expected. -- Cockcroft

10. Davante Adams, WR, Los Angeles Rams
Adams had nine targets in the win over the Eagles; however, he caught four passes for only 32 yards (7.2 points). With Nacua back from injury (12 targets), Adams is set to stay as a lower-tier WR2/Flex for the Week 5 matchup versus the Bills. -- Bowen

Injury impact

Ladd McConkey, WR, Los Angeles Chargers

What we know: After dealing with a foot injury during the practice week, McConkey suffered a setback and was ruled out for the day early in the third quarter.

What's next: Marquez Valdes-Scantling saw an uptick in work following McConkey's absence, but Quentin Johnston and Tre' Harris would be the top two receivers if McConkey needs to miss Week 5. It's a subpar matchup against the Broncos -- though their cornerbacks did suffer injuries of their own -- for that game and the struggling Broncos passing game should be avoided. -- Cockcroft

Rashee Rice, WR, Kansas City Chiefs

What we know: After catching a pass in the first quarter, Rice suffered a hamstring injury, and he did not return to the game.

What's next: The Chiefs head into the bye next week, so we'll wait for updates on Rice ahead of the Week 6 matchup versus the Chargers. With Tyquan Thornton also going down with a severe ankle injury, the Chiefs are thin at wide receiver. As of now, Xavier Worthy will move into an elevated role, and we could see more volume for Jalen Royals. Stay tuned. -- Bowen

Saquon Barkley, RB, Philadelphia Eagles

What we know: Barkley suffered a hamstring injury in the first quarter versus the Rams, and he did not return. Barkley had just three touches, finishing with 10 total yards (2.0 points).

What's next: Eagles No. 2 Tank Bigsby replaced Barkley, rushing for 55 yards on 14 carries. However, Bigsby left the game in the fourth quarter because of a lower-body injury. Let's keep an eye on updates this week for Barkley and Bigsby as the Eagles prep for their Week 5 matchup at Jacksonville. --Bowen

Lamar Jackson, QB, Baltimore Ravens

What we know: Jackson injured his ankle late in the second quarter on a sack versus the Titans, and he did not return. Jackson scored 18.8 points in only one half Sunday, throwing for 222 yards and two touchdowns, while rushing for 20 yards. Tyler Huntley replaced Jackson to start the second half.

What's next: If Jackson can't return for the Week 5 game at Atlanta, Huntley will get the start. Huntley made two starts in 2025, scoring 14 or more points in each, and I believe Ravens offensive coordinator Declan Doyle will set up his quarterback on play-action concepts early. Still, we should expect a run-heavy approach, which keeps Derrick Henry in the RB1 mix, while managers can play Zay Flowers as a WR2. -- Bowen

Ja'Marr Chase, WR, Cincinnati Bengals

What we know: Chase left in the second quarter because of a concussion suffered when Jaguars CB Jarrian Jones committed a facemask penalty and LB Ventrell Miller immediately afterward delivered a hard hit to the star wide receiver. Chase didn't return to the game.

What's next: It's never easy for players to swiftly clear the NFL's concussion protocol, so Chase's status for Week 5 is iffy, and bear in mind that the Bengals could rest him regardless, knowing he'd get an extra week's rest with the Week 6 bye. Tee Higgins would elevate to No. 1 receiver status if Chase sits, and Dohnte Meyers, who played 90% of snaps, ran 54 routes and had 15.2 fantasy points Sunday, could be a one-week sleeper if pressed into starting duty. -- Cockcroft

D.J. Moore, WR, Buffalo Bills

What we know: Moore injured his shoulder while diving for a catch in the first half versus the Patriots, and he did not return to the game.

What's next: If Moore is out for the Week 5 matchup at the Rams, Khalil Shakir will get more steady volume as a catch-and-run target for Josh Allen, while Keon Coleman provides big-play ability. Shakir caught seven of eight targets for 82 yards Sunday (13.2 points). Coleman scored 23.6 points, catching six of seven targets for 119 yards and a score. -- Bowen

Marcus Mariota, QB, Washington Commanders

What we know: Mariota reinjured the medial collateral ligament in his right knee, an injury he initially suffered during the Commanders' preseason opener, after Colts DE Laiatu Latu landed on the quarterback's lower leg on a first-quarter sack. Commanders coach Dan Quinn said coming out of halftime that Mariota was done for the day, a signal that this might be a multiweek injury.

What's next: With Jayden Daniels also sidelined, the Commanders turned to rookie seventh-round pick Athan Kaliakmanis, who went 15-for-33 passing for 186 yards, one touchdown, one interception and 11.04 fantasy points. Daniels (elbow dislocation) resumed practicing this week and has a chance to return for Week 5, but the Commanders will be in rough shape offensively otherwise. Even with a decent matchup against the Giants, Commanders skill players should be avoided if Daniels and Mariota are absent. -- Cockcroft

stories.headline: Jackson Chourio walk-off single lifts Brewers to 2-0 NLDS edge
stories.summary: Jackson Chourio hit a two-run single off Padres closer Mason Miller with two outs in the ninth inning as the Brewers rallied past the Padres for a 2-0 NLDS lead.
stories.body:
MILWAUKEE -- Jackson Chourio hit a two-run single off hard-throwing Mason Miller with two outs in the ninth inning and the Milwaukee Brewers rallied past the San Diego Padres for the second time in 20 hours, a 4-3 victory Sunday for a 2-0 National League Division Series lead.

Miller entered with a 3-2 lead, trying for his first six-out save since 2024. He retired the side in order in the eighth and, after a leadoff groundout in the ninth, issued his first career postseason walks to Christian Yelich and Sal Frelick.

Andrew Vaughn flied out and pinch hitter Gary Sanchez walked on a full count.

A night after sparking Milwaukee's comeback with a tying, two-run homer in the third inning, the 22-year-old Chourio lined a 101.3 mph fastball up the middle and past second baseman Jake Cronenworth's attempt for a diving backhand stop.

The ball bounced into center field as Yelich ran across the plate to tie it, with Frelick sliding in head-first to win it, easily beating center fielder Jackson Merrill's throw.

San Diego, which entered the postseason with 20 wins in its past 23 games, has back-to-back losses for the first time since Sept. 1-2. The Padres will try to keep their season alive Tuesday when the best-of-five series resumes in San Diego.

Milwaukee is a win from a second straight NL Championship Series appearance as it chases its first World Series title.

Chourio also made a key defensive play in the opener when Ty France hit a potential go-ahead homer in the ninth inning only for the ball to strike a cable on the roof of American Family Field and land in Chourio's glove at the left-field warning track.

Miller, baseball's top closer, threw 40 pitches -- his most since 2023. He topped 100 mph with 18 pitches, the fastest a 103.5 mph offering that Chourio fouled.

Milwaukee didn't have a baserunner against Padres starter Michael King until the fifth inning and matched a season high with three errors as San Diego scored a pair of unearned runs.

With the roof open Sunday, France hit an RBI single in the first and another a run-scoring single for a 3-1 lead in the seventh after third baseman David Hamilton bobbled Fernando Tatis Jr.'s grounder for an error.

Frelick had an RBI single in the fifth after Yelich doubled.

Milwaukee closed to 3-2 in the seventh when Garrett Mitchell scored from third as Cronenworth bobbled Hamilton's grounder and then threw past first for a double error.

stories.headline: Pistons' Jalen Duren happy to return despite prolonged talks
stories.summary: Despite a prolonged negotiation that appeared to turn sour at times, Jalen Duren said he is relieved and excited to return to Detroit.
stories.body:
Jalen Duren was both relieved and excited after signing a new five-year, $200 million deal to return to the Detroit Pistons after a contract negotiation that he said took "longer than both he and the organization anticipated."

But during his first news conference after signing his new deal, he wanted to clarify narratives that emerged during the negotiation that he said did not represent how he felt about the team, repeating that he was happy in Detroit and excited to return to the team.

"Detroit has become a home for me, this is where I live full-time," Duren told reporters at the team's practice facility on Sunday afternoon. "The city has embraced me as well as I've embraced the city.

"This process took way longer than any of us really wanted. Longer than I wanted, and I'm sure longer than the organization wanted. But [the Pistons] have a job to do as well as my team and my agency have a job to do to make the best outcome for both sides. I feel like we've done that."

Duren missed media day and the first few practices of training camp this week after a four-month long standoff between he and the Pistons over the value of his new contract. They eventually came to an agreement on a fully guaranteed contract late Thursday night, ahead of the deadline for him to accept a one-year qualifying offer.

On Sunday, sitting next to team president of basketball operations Trajan Langdon, Duren said he wanted to be in Detroit for the rest of his career.

"There's a business component that it took me time to realize and understand because this is my first time going through it," the 22-year old All-NBA center said. "I can admit that I have flaws. We all do and we're here to work on it.

"I don't think this should be a negative outlook or looked at as something bad has happened. I think we look at it as something great has happened. I'm locked in with a team and a core who has potential that's going through the roof and I'm super excited for what's to come."

The standoff over Duren's contract came following the best regular season of the young center's career. He averaged a career high in points (19.5), made his first All-Star team and was named to the All-NBA third team as the Pistons became the top seed in the Eastern Conference. But he struggled mightily in the postseason, dropping to 10.2 points per game in 14 playoff games before Detroit's second-round exit.

Duren said he took a step back to get his head right following a postseason he described as "humbling," and he acknowledged his own silence allowed narratives to emerge in his absence. But he said he stayed focused in the offseason on getting better and acknowledging his flaws.

"Last season was some of my highest moments in my career and some of my lowest," Duren said. "I'm willing to acknowledge that. And I'm willing to turn that frustration and that anger and whatever I felt toward my play and how things may have ended, I've learned instead of exerting my energy in being mad, exerting my energy into bettering my craft."

stories.headline: Lacob lauds Williams as world's best after Valkyries' Game 1 win
stories.summary: Gabby Williams scored 25 points and played lockdown defense in a performance that led Valkyries owner Joe Lacob to declare her the "best player in the world."
stories.body:
SAN FRANCISCO -- Golden State Valkyries owner Joe Lacob walked through the tunnels of Chase Center following the Valkyries 71-60 win over the Las Vegas Aces in Game 1 of the WNBA semifinals with a message he wanted to get off of his chest.

"Print this: Gabby Williams is the best player in the world," Lacob told ESPN.

Williams scored a team-high 25 points on Sunday afternoon, and scored or assisted on 36 of the Valkyries' points. On the other end, she held the Aces to just 29% on 4-of-14 shooting as the primary defender. Williams, who also had 11 rebounds and five assists, became the second player all-time with 25 points, 10 rebounds and five assists in a playoff game against the Aces. She is also the first Valkyries player to have a 25-10-5 playoff game.

After arriving in Golden State during the offseason, Williams has taken her play to another level with the Valkyries -- finishing second in Defensive Player of the Year voting, and also adding to her offensive game. So far, she's averaging 25 points during the playoffs, which is the third-highest scoring average of the postseason. Only Wilson and Arike Ogunbowale have scored more.

Early in the game on Sunday, Williams felt that the Aces were trying to make her uncomfortable, throwing a mixture of coverages at her. That's when she made sure she was intentional about getting everyone else involved.

"There are five players on the court," Williams said. "We were running really well in transition, so I found (Kayla Thornton) a couple times, and things started to open up on their own."

The Valkyries' ability to get out and run was fueled by their performance on the boards. Golden State outrebounded Las Vegas 52-25 -- the second-largest difference by any team in a playoff game in WNBA history. They also held the Aces to a season-low in scoring.

The Aces made pushes, clawing back from down by as much as 11, but they never took away Golden State's momentum and couldn't get their deficit below five points down the stretch of the game.

"All we talked about the last 48 hours was rebounding and blocking them out, and we did not do that. Period," Aces coach Becky Hammon said. "The good news is, we played like ass and only lost by 10."

A'ja Wilson finished with 24 points on 8-of-21 field goal shooting and went 8-of-11 from the free-throw line. Chelsea Gray and Jackie Young combined for 25 points.

"I've competed against A'ja my entire career, and she will go down in history as the best player to ever do it," Williams said. "This is what you dream about. You dream to play against players like that. Going up against them is all I care about ... I just want to win."

Williams rolled her eyes when she heard what Lacob said about her, but the belief he has poured into her is the reason she is leading the Valkyries in their playoff push. During every game, she seeks out a fist bump from the owner to "absorb" some of his energy. When she watches replays of the game, she zooms in to see his spirited reaction to big plays.

"There she is," Lacob yelled when he saw Williams standing in the hallway after the game, his arms open for a hug. "Best player in the world. No one is saying it, but they need to start saying it."

stories.headline: AFL Draft Combine 2026: Key takeaways, results, times from from the weekend
stories.summary: Who stood out at the 2026 AFL Draft Combine? One record tumbled, and others posted some impressive results. Jasper Chellappah was on hand, and here are his big takeaways from the weekend.
stories.body:
There's an open pool pick one favourite to come out of the AFL Draft combine, while a key forward has bolstered his top 10 chances with a record-shattering performance in the final chance for prospects to enhance their credentials.

The 63 most in-demand juniors converged on Melbourne across the week for club and media interviews, medicals and athletic testing at the national combine. It's a frantic week of up to 18 club interviews, media appearances and athletic scrutiny under the watchful eyes of recruiters.

Players to forego testing due to injury included nominal pick one Dougie Cochrane (knee management), top five Dragons duo Arki Butler (hamstring) and Gus Teixeira (calf, foot), plus top 10 fancies Mitch Harris (ankle) and Ethan Matthews (foot). Marlon Neocleous, Kodah Edwards, Jackson Phillips and Noah Williams were other highly-rated prospects to miss physical testing.

The running vertical jump record was matched then broken within five minutes and Lachie Hicks's elite pedigree was on display, finishing second in the 2km time trial, ninth in the 20m sprint and first in the agility test.

These are the biggest winners and dominating headlines to come from an important week in the AFL Draft calendar.

High flyer's exploits place him in top 10 range
Sam Gayfer shattered the running vertical jump combine record on Saturday. Previously held by Leek Aleer at 107cm, the leading key forward prospect gapped that mark with a soaring 114cm on Saturday. To put that leap into perspective, it would sit comfortably at fourth all-time at the NFL Draft combine and third all-time at the NBA Draft combine. It's no wonder testers at the state netball centre asked the 18-year-old to redo his jump and double-check their accuracy.

Adding his height, wingspan and 114cm leap together and Gayfer can pluck a football four metres off the ground.

The nephew of Collingwood 1990 premiership defender Mick, Gayfer has all-world athleticism that shows up in the tape. He took one of the great marks out of the goal square earlier this year against the Suns Academy, soaring onto shoulders and holding on for a moment that will be replayed throughout his career.

He's been a steady riser throughout the year, impressing most through the national championships as Vic Metro's spearhead and kicking 10 goals from four games to solidify his first-round credentials.

Now, he's a top 10 prospect with clubs including Melbourne, St Kilda and Collingwood all in for the 194cm tall.

Open pool No. 1 favourite emerges
You wouldn't know it speaking to him, but Drever now has his nose in front in the race to be Essendon's selection at the top of the draft board. The humble Ballarat local has enjoyed an injury-free season, propelling himself to the top of the board for the Dons in the open pool.

Drever plays a modern style through the midfield, driving his legs with the acceleration that saw him finish with a top five time in the 20m sprint. It's become a trademark of his to burst out of clearance and kick long-running goals as he breaks the paint of the 50m arc.

At 188cm, Drever has the size to play inside and the defensive appetite to tackle and chase. He averaged 6.5 tackles for the Rebels and maintained his consistent excellence across wins and losses. Drever's 6:27 minute 2km showed the power athlete is on his way to building a tank as a full-time on-baller at the next level.

While Essendon has informed Port Adelaide of their intentions of bidding on NGA star Dougie Cochrane with the first overall selection, they are still deciding on their selection between Drever, Arki Butler, Heath Mellody, Harry Van Hattum and Gus Teixeira in the open pool.

Walker puts competitiveness on show in 2km time trial
Cody Walker is bound for the Blues and has little left to prove after a sensational season with Carlton's VFL side. But that didn't stop him from breaking through his personal best time in the 2km on Thursday.

"My PB was 6:13... I was just feeling good and thought I'd try the best time I can," Walker told ESPN.

The midfielder smashed through that time with a 6:04, good for third at the combine. It was a feat made even more impressive by being in the second-fastest group and having no one by his side in the final lap. He finished nine seconds ahead of the rest of the field and admitted to finding his own personal motivation with no one to challenge him up front.

"I'm a competitor, I do want to see where I'm at right now compared to three months later when I do a 2km at the club.

"I just want to compete against the best talent."

Walker's name has been up in lights for the better part of four years as Blues fans keenly tracked his progress. An Echuca native, he made the move down to Melbourne permanently this year and has been into the club full-time including game reviews, line meetings and team dinners.

With Cochrane set to be the No. 1 pick with a bid via Essendon, Walker could slide deeper into the top five on draft night despite his enormous year in the VFL and national championships.

Melbourne at pick six looms as the last spot where he could attract a bid, and it would be good news for Carlton who lost their 10% discount on matching a points bid with their epic run into finals under Josh Fraser.

Holding their own selection and Sydney's first rounder via the Charlie Curnow trade last year, the Blues can match an outright bid at pick four onwards with selections 11 and 16, but risk going into deficit on their first-rounder next year if a bid on Walker comes any earlier from Essendon or West Coast.

Nephew of Eagles great returns after ACL injury
Koby LeCras has endured a tumultuous year. From best on ground amongst the top talent of the AFL Academy to a partial ACL tear the following week in his WAFL debut, the nephew of small forward Mark thought his season was over. But after initial scans cleared him of a full rupture, the 192cm forward circled the draft combine on his calendar.

After just six weeks of full running, he suited up for the 2km run six months on from his injury and posted an impressive 6:23 minutes.

"Going into it, I had 6:25 written on my hand. To get away with a couple seconds, it felt good," he told ESPN after the run.

"You look at Gryan Miers, you can rush it. Being my draft year, I've got a lot more footy to play than just this year.

"Whether it is combine or day one of pre-season I definitely wanted to be back for something."

LeCras was given the all clear from doctors leading into the combine and put in a stellar performance to remind recruiters of his talent. That final full game for the AFL Academy was a three-goal performance off a wing, showcasing his athletic prowess reminiscent of Ollie Dempsey pushing hard forward for Geelong. He boasts the finesse and craft around goal of his uncle, but has ambitions of becoming a genuine key forward at AFL level.

LeCras's range starts towards the end of the first round, and despite the untimely knee injury clubs expect him to be snapped up well within the second round of the draft after his diligent rehab.

Long jumper leaning towards footy after dominant combine
Mason McGroder has a big decision to make in the coming weeks. The gun long jumper already has a bronze medal from the U20s world championships at 16 years of age, and backed it up this year with a silver medal in August, but is leaning towards an AFL career after blitzing the national combine.

McGroder posted the fastest 20m sprint of any prospect to test and did it comfortably on Saturday morning. He was also second amongst all prospects in the standing and running vertical jumps to further enhance his stocks, with clubs keen to get a look at the athletic prowess of the Swans Academy defender.

At 194cm he can play a multitude of roles but has looked most at home in defence where his natural athleticism allows him to close distance quickly and impact in the air. Similarly to Max King 12 months ago, Sydney will be keen to lock away McGroder if he does choose footy and let the high-upside teen develop in their VFL side.

McGroder is awaiting collegiate offers for a potential long jumping career before he makes his call, with the 2032 Brisbane Olympics another consideration as he weighs up his options.

stories.headline: Bahrain GP was the worst indictment of F1's new engine regs yet
stories.summary: There was a lot to love about Sunday's race. But it will forever be overshadowed by the mess caused by the new F1 engines.
stories.body:
SEPANG, Malaysia -- The Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia already had a farcical name. Formula 1's unnecessarily complicated hybrid engines ensured the race will be remembered as one of the biggest farces in the sport's recent history.

F1's current engines, which feature a near 50-50 split between internal combustion energy and electrical battery elements, are already considered the biggest mistake the sport has made in recent times. Whenever they are consigned to the scrapheap, the foremost memories will be of Sunday's two formation laps in the rain.

"LOL, look at this," was all a laughing Max Verstappen could say over the radio as his Red Bull approached a handful of cars whose engines had simply shut down. His car had already done the same at the front of the pack a couple of minutes earlier.

It was an apt use of modern day slang: Laugh out loud was all you could really do. Collectively, and due to a perfect storm of circumstances, F1's cars had all ground to a walking speed, one after the other. The first attempt at starting the race -- already delayed 40 minutes, because these F1 cars cannot race in extremely wet conditions -- was aborted, with another wait to allow the 11 teams to download and implement a software update from the governing FIA.

"Horrible," said reigning world champion Lando Norris after the race. "It just proves that we shouldn't have any of that stuff on the electronic side".

George Russell, who also dealt with a heartbreaking late engine failure which has all but handed Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli the 2026 championship, said, "The whole day was a bit of a faff. It didn't feel very F1 today".

Carlos Sainz summed up the situation best of all: "I think F1 needs to have a hard look at themselves and see how we ended up in this situation."

There's a lot to still love about F1 in 2026, and some of it was on show towards the end of Sunday's chaotic race. But the absolute worst of the sport was also showcased in brutal fashion before a competitive lap had even been completed.

What exactly happened?
As well as new-look cars and new V6 turbo hybrid engines, this year introduced a new set of Pirelli tyres. The Italian company's wet-weather tyres have been a question-mark all season, however: bar a February test behind closed doors in Spain and wet-weather tests for Red Bull, Racing Bulls and Ferrari earlier in the year, no teams had done any meaningful runs on the intermediate or full wets prior to this weekend.

The FIA immediately delayed the start as the weather intensified, with a nearby thunderstorm also complicating things. Several teams briefly lost their weather radars on the pit wall, while some of the marshal panels lining the circuit briefly stopped working.

At 3:40 p.m. local time, 40 minutes after the race was supposed to start, the FIA attempted to get things underway with two formation laps behind the safety car, followed by a standing start from the grid. The rain had started easing off and the track was wet, but it looked as though race control was going to make a go of it. But those formation laps were always going to be an exercise in extreme caution.

Several corners into the first formation lap is where things started going wrong, when the cars encountered a software bug baked into the algorithms that dictate F1's new complicated engines. During rain, for safety reasons, engine modes run at a maximum deployment of 250 kilowatts of deployment in certain sectors, down from 350kW in dry conditions. Once Verstappen, leading the pack but tiptoeing around on the cold intermediates, dropped below a speed of 50 km/h, the algorithms dictating the behaviour of his engine started having problems: essentially, the MGU-K no longer kicked in to feed power into his low-revving engine. The restriction on the car's hybrid-electric component is meant to prevent teams from effectively using it as a traction control device at the start of a race; this time, however, the combination of not running on wet tires with an extremely wet tarmac meant drivers were applying much less throttle than normal.

The algorithm did not spot the difference, so kicked in. With the additional power boost locked out, the internal combustion engine was effectively dying without a surge of recovery power from the electrical side.

You wouldn't be the only one confused by this: F1 drivers have said this year's debriefs with engineers are longer and more complicated than ever. Many have spoken about their engines behaving in radically different ways lap to lap, as self-learning algorithms kick in power at different points.

In the moment, what was happening was unclear: Some thought Verstappen simply had an engine issue.

"There was nothing going on," he said later. "That was the problem. It was just like driving at, what, 35 km/h, going uphill, actually losing speed. So, yeah, I don't know exactly, because when you go too low in speed and too low RPM, for whatever reason, then it just bogs down. Normally it takes one or two seconds and it comes back."

But this time, the power did not come back. Verstappen's car was slowing so dramatically, which meant the cars behind him bunched up. But the rules state you cannot overtake the car in front on a formation lap.

"I triggered it first and then I look in my mirror, I just see... I was like, "Wait, are they waiting for me or what's going on...?" Verstappen said.

Those behind were, in fact, waiting. The same thing happened to Lewis Hamilton's Ferrari, in second position, shortly after his car also dropped below the all-important 50 km/h benchmark.

"It was like the Lego race," Hamilton joked later, referring to the viral pre-race spectacle during the Miami Grand Prix in May.

While Verstappen somehow managed to avoid coming to a complete standstill, Hamilton's ground to a halt. The seven-time world champion had to restart his Ferrari's power unit on the pit straight. But unlike with Verstappen, cars slowly started passing Hamilton as he plummeted down the order.

"It was insane," said current championship leader Antonelli. "At some point we were five-wide in the straight, because we couldn't understand what was going on."

Hamilton's Ferrari seemed to suffer the most extreme version of the engine issue: By the time he did stop completely, he was half way down the order, and Audi, Williams, Racing Bulls and other teams' cars were facing similar issues around him. It was this scene a laughing Verstappen would later drive past. The start procedure was canceled, effectively a red flag.

And here is where the lack of wet tire usage this year had caught the FIA out.

"We didn't manage to test the software as extensively as we would have liked, because there's been very little wet running this year," the governing body's single seater chief Nikolas Tombazis explained in a rare trip to the media pen after the race.

"There was a bit of a combination of circumstances which caused this bug to kick in. Basically, [on] the formation lap, some cars went very slowly, almost came to a standstill. There was a bit of a concertina effect between cars, and some cars almost stopped completely. That bug prevented the power from being redeployed, and for the cars to start again. I think if we had had a bit more testing, we probably would have managed to catch it in time, and not have such a situation.

"Once the problem happened, our guys realised very quickly what was happening, and had to work under a lot of time pressure for an update to the software, which was issued to the teams, and the teams had to install it on their cars.

The FIA later gave a simpler statement on what had happened, blaming a perfect storm of various factors. The governing body said "an unprecedented combination of low engine speed, low-grip conditions, wet-weather energy management settings and the Sepang circuit's sector configuration led to an unintended loss of power for a number of cars".

The remedy was a software update -- code Tombazis admitted was a "cobbled up, hurried solution." Rewriting and sending the new code to the teams to install in their systems led to another delay. It meant the worst of the rain also disappeared, we got only a handful of laps on the intermediates and the prospect of a genuine wet-weather classic disappeared.

If you still need another way to think about it: The 11 teams competing in the pinnacle of motorsport hit Ctrl+Alt+Delete and installed a software update to race safely again.

The fallout
The FIA did apologize afterward for the chaos.

"All of that took about 20 minutes," Tombazis said. "It may have felt like five hours for spectators waiting in a race and for everybody else, which is understandable. And we are sorry about that. But I think it was quite a fast reaction given the problem."

The sport's governing body could easily direct critics toward a race ultimately full of incidents and overtaking. And, fair enough: Sepang was an entertaining spectacle.

Verstappen returned to the top step for the first time this season. Hamilton turned in a supreme drive for third after gambling incorrectly on slick tires over intermediates, which had him over a minute down on the lead early. Antonelli now looks certain to become the sport's youngest ever champion after Russell's late DNF (and the engine penalties likely to come with it).

It was a fitting return for the brilliant Sepang circuit, too. Yet, the engines are such a step in the wrong direction it's hard to look past it.

"That's what happens when you have these engines," Verstappen said. He's been outspoken about the regs since the first time he drove a 2026 car, so it's perhaps not a surprise what he said next.

"With a V8 you don't have these problems".

F1's current rules were drawn up over a period of years, and the promise of the V6 turbo hybrid engines was making the sport more appealing to new manufacturers -- Audi this year, General Motors by the end of the decade. But the price to lure two new manufacturers to the sport does not seem worth it so far.

F1 will make small tweaks to the engines over the next two years, shifting the 50-50 split closer towards a 60-40 split in favor of conventional combustion power over the electrical elements by 2028. But many in the paddock believe it will not be enough to make racing feel normal again.

Sainz, who has been vocal about the situation, believes the sport has to learn from Sepang. "It is clear the regs are extremely complicated for the drivers, for the teams, for the PUs, for the manufacturers," he said after the race. "Again, my only question mark is: Who, five years ago, decided that this was the direction to go?

"The FIA and F1 are doing the best they can with what was decided four or five years ago, but clearly what was decided four or five years ago is wrong."

A silver lining to end on: Sunday's engine farce may end up accelerating the push to drop V6s in favour of V8s at the earliest possible opportunity.

Whenever that day is, it cannot be soon enough.

stories.headline: Kyle Connor scores a pair of power-play goals as Jets squeak past Red Wings 3-2
stories.summary: — Kyle Connor scored two of Winnipeg's three power-play goals and added an assist on the third as the Jets held off the Detroit Red Wings 3-2 on Sunday.
stories.body:
DETROIT -- — Kyle Connor scored two of Winnipeg's three power-play goals and added an assist on the third as the Jets held off the Detroit Red Wings 3-2 on Sunday.


Cole Perfetti scored the Jets' other goal and had two assists, while Josh Morrissey also had two assists. Stuart Skinner made 33 saves in Winnipeg's first victory. The Jets lost to Boston in overtime in their season opener on Friday.


Viktor Arvidsson and Emmitt Finnie scored for the Red Wings and John Gibson stopped 24 saves. Detroit was blanked 2-0 by the New York Rangers in its opener on Friday.


Prominent members of the United States' gold-medal squad at the Milan Cortina Olympics were not on the ice. Detroit center Dylan Larkin was sidelined with an upper-body injury, while Winnipeg goaltender Connor Hellebuyck remained on the suspended/inactive list. Both players have requested trades from their teams.


Detroit defenseman Simon Edvinsson (unsigned) and forward Marco Kasper (upper body) also missed the game.


The Jets took advantage of unsportsmanlike conduct penalties against Keegan Kolesar and J.T. Compher in the first period on goals by Perfetti and Connor.


Connor scored his second power-play goal from the right circle during the second period. Arvidsson ended the Red Wings' scoring drought with 3:08 left in the period.


Finnie's goal at 4:56 of the third cut the Jets' lead to 3-2. The Red Wings failed to take advantage of a late power-play opportunity and Skinner made a nifty save against Lucas Raymond in the final minute to preserve the Jets' lead.


Up next
Jets: Visit Pittsburgh on Monday.


Red Wings: Host Ottawa on Tuesday.

stories.summary: Arsenal, Real Madrid and Bayern Munich are all chasing Juventus winger Kenan Yildiz. Transfer Talk has the latest.
stories.body:
Arsenal, Real Madrid and Bayern Munich are all chasing Juventus winger Kenan Yildiz. Plus, could Endrick leave Real Madrid for AC Milan?

Join us for the latest transfer news and rumors from around the globe.

Transfers home page | Men's summer grades | Women's grades

Trending rumors

- Real Madrid are pushing for Kenan Yildiz with Arsenal and Bayern Munich also looking at the Juventus winger, reports Corriere dello Sport. Juve have been demanding at least €100 million for the 21-year-old for a year, but Madrid are reigniting their interest in him with the view to a move in the summer. They would want to pit him and Vinícius Júnior against each other, while Arsenal see the Turkiye international as the answer to their lack of options on the left and Bayern have been watching him from afar since his departure.

- AC Milan are planning to make another attempt to sign Real Madrid striker Endrick after being unable to bring him in during the summer, reports La Gazzetta dello Sport. Madrid boss Jose Mourinho had initially refused to let the 20-year-old leave, but he has made just one substitute appearance this season that lasted four minutes. Milan's main competition from within Italy for the Brazil international is Roma, while Aston Villa were also unsuccessful in their efforts to bring him in last summer.

- Barcelona are willing to let Alejandro Balde leave on loan in January with Manchester United among the clubs interested in the left-back, according to TEAMtalk. The 22-year-old has fallen down the pecking order in Hansi Flick's squad and has only got onto the pitch once so far this season, playing the last 12 minutes in a 7-2 win over Racing Santander. The Spaniard's camp and intermediaries are already working hard to find a solution for him, while the Blaugrana could look to bring in a new left-back in 2027.

- Liverpool center back Giovanni Leoni is the latest name La Gazzetta dello Sport have linked with Juventus, as I Bianconeri aim to introduce young Italian talent to their squad. The Serie A side have turned their attention away from the likes of Arsenal's Riccardo Calafiori and Chelsea's Marco Palestra, who are now seen as unattainable, and had already made enquiries about a loan for Leoni in recent months. Liverpool haven't opened the door to the 19-year-old leaving, but Juventus aren't giving up on him.

- Barcelona are interested in 18-year-old FC Twente center back Ruud Nijstad, reports transfer journalist Fabrizio Romano. They are monitoring the young Dutchman, having already made contact about him in August but ultimately being told that a transfer wasn't possible as Twente wanted him to be a key player for them. More clubs are showing an interest in Nijstad and have started travelling to scout him.

- Real Madrid are among the clubs who could move to sign Manchester United attacker JJ Gabriel, according to Spanish newspaper AS. Various clubs across Europe are looking at the 15-year-old after it was made clear that he wants to leave the Red Devils and requested a transfer. Bayern Munich have emerged as major rivals for his signature and Barcelona have gained momentum in recent days. Man United have leaked that they will take legal action against any club that negotiates with Gabriel.

Other rumors
- Arsenal, Barcelona, AC Milan, and Juventus all want to sign 15-year-old Borussia Dortmund midfielder Justin Ejodamen. (TEAMtalk)

- Tottenham Hotspur have no interest in letting Micky van de Ven leave as Liverpool prepare to move for the centre-back next year. (Football Insider)

stories.headline: UFC 332 takeaways: Talbott, Silva validate their top billing
stories.summary: Payton Talbott finished another former champion in Deiveson Figueiredo on a night full of knockouts at UFC 332.
stories.body:
The options were plenty for performance bonuses after UFC 332 in Salt Lake City. The fight card set a UFC record for knockouts with 11, and nine came in the first round. The most resounding KO went to men's bantamweight Payton Talbott in the co-main event. He came out strong, sending former champion Deiveson Figueiredo to the canvas twice before finishing him a little over two minutes into the fight. The win is Talbott's second in a row over a former champion and likely means big things ahead for him, but the loss for Figueiredo doesn't do anything to minimize his legacy in the UFC.

The main event, which received prefight chatter over whether it was worthy of a headlining slot, was high energy but mostly one-sided. Natalia Silva, the No. 1 women's flyweight contender, earned her first UFC championship with a unanimous decision over Wang Cong. The 29-year-old joins men's flyweight Joshua Van as the only UFC champions under 30.

Was the main event criticism validated?
The UFC took heat on social media for booking Silva vs. Wang in a main event on a numbered card. Silva was at the front of a long line of women's flyweight title contenders, no question, but it's fair to say Wang, unranked by ESPN and outside the top five in the UFC's own rankings, jumped the queue.

But while I'm on board with a lot of the criticism the UFC receives for its matchmaking, especially at a championship level, I understand what the fight promotion was going for in this case: The UFC was trying to set up a couple of possible storylines involving Valentina Shevchenko, who vacated the women's flyweight title to make the Silva-Wang title fight a possibility after suffering an undisclosed injury that will sideline her for "up to one year."

Why Wang? She might not have an extensive UFC résumé, but she beat Shevchenko in a kickboxing match in 2015. Their history is not unlike that of Alex Pereira and Israel Adesanya, who met twice in kickboxing, with Pereira winning both and knocking out Adesanya in one of those fights. It provided a setup for their UFC rivalry.

A Wang vs. Shevchenko angle became moot, as things turned out, because Silva was too much for the Chinese fighter to handle. Wang came in with a 10-1 MMA record, but she had zero fights against top-10 flyweights, and it showed. Silva, by contrast, came in having defeated former UFC champions (Jessica Andrade, Alexa Grasso and Rose Namajunas) in each of her past three fights.

Silva was too fast, too elusive and too precise with her punches and kicks. Wang had no answers, looked lost and couldn't get her offense going until the fifth round, when it was too late. Not to vindicate the prefight matchmaking criticism, but this sure was a lopsided and not-so-fiery bout, one that got booed by a crowd that had been treated to a UFC-record 11 knockouts on the night.

So now the 125-pound division is left with the Silva vs. Shevchenko storyline we were expecting to see before Shevchenko was injured. It will be interesting to see how Silva's speed holds up when she meets her predecessor with the belt, and how differently she'll fight when up against an opponent with a strong grappling game. Oddly, that wasn't even addressed in Silva's postfight interview in the cage. Shevchenko's name wasn't even mentioned. Now, that is a UFC decision worth questioning. -- Jeff Wagenheim

Quick thanks to Figueiredo

MMA loves to move quickly, and it's ready to move very fast with Talbott. Talbott is everything MMA could want in a prospect, and his future is very bright.

So before we all take off on the Talbott train (as we inevitably will), let's take a moment to shout out one of the most exciting flyweights of all time, Figueiredo.

Let's be honest, Figueiredo was always a borrowed bantamweight. He struggled to make 125 pounds, and most of the sport was happy to see him ditch the weight cut in 2023, but he was also undersized at 135.

It's easy to forget now, as UFC men's flyweight champion Van has taken the sport by storm -- but the flyweight division was still in a precarious position when Figueiredo made his mark in 2020. Henry Cejudo saved the division by knocking out TJ Dillashaw in 2018, but then eventually vacated a weight class the UFC seriously considered shutting down. Figueiredo picked up where Cejudo left off, saving the division with his one-punch knockout power and (frankly) villain charisma. He played the role of "bad guy" in his back-to-back fights against Joseph Benavidez in 2020, as well as his four-fight rivalry with Brandon Moreno.

It was inevitable when he moved up in weight, but for a three-year period, Figueiredo was the exact figure the flyweight division needed. The 38-year-old's career is undoubtedly coming to an end soon, but Figueiredo was not just a terrific fighter and champion in his prime, he will forever be remembered as a significant hero of flyweight MMA. -- Brett Okamoto
